title: TA8-14349
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXX XXXX XXXXXX, (the "claimant" or the "XXXX"), is a 34 year-old resident of the West Bank holding a passport issued by the Palestinian Authority and is claiming refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration Refugee Protection Act (the "Act").1 Allegations
The claimant's allegations are found in his Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative.2 Briefly, he alleged as follows:

The claimant comes from XXXX, Palestine. He is XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXX Military Service in Ramallah. His duties included XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. In the case of the prisoners, XXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

The XXXX received two telephone demands to assist anti-PA elements, such as Hamas or the Al-jihad Al-islami movement by finding that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXX. He notified his supervisor, a XXXXXXXXX in the PA military, after each call.

The claimant felt the second call to be the more serious as the caller mentioned Hamas and the death of someone in the intelligence prison. The caller blamed the XXXX, although he cannot recall the name or circumstance, and felt the claim "absurd". Again, he notified his supervisor, in a panic, but was told merely to be cautious, which did not assist the claimant in knowing what to do.

A month after the second call, his home was shot up by unknown attackers. The next day he "...received a call from the same unidentified Hamas representative..." that, although he had survived, the next time the bullet would surely hit him. He notified his supervisor who did nothing, so he left Palestine for Canada on XXXX 2008.
The claimant made his claim for protection in Canada on 1 August 2008, just over one month later. Determination

The panel has determined that the claimant is not a Convention refugee in that he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution in Palestine based on a Convention ground. The panel also determines that the claimant is not a person in need of protection as there are no substantial grounds to believe that the claimant's removal to Palestine will subject him to a danger of torture and, on a balance of probabilities, he does not face a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Analysis
The determinative issues in this claim are credibility and state protection. Identity

The claimant's identity as a national of Palestine has been established by his testimony and the claimant's documents, including his passport from the Palestinian Authority (PA).3 Also, the claimant's identity, XXXXXXXXXXX who worked for the military, was established4 by the claimant's testimony and the materials disclosed.5 Nexus

For the claimant to be a Convention refugee, his fear of persecution must be by reason of one of the five grounds enumerated in the Convention refugee definition. Counsel suggested that this claim be considered under imputed political opinion. I find that the claimant's fear of persecution is linked to one of the five grounds, as submitted.

The claimant alleged that, should he return to Palestine, he would be killed by Hamas or its anti-PA allies for not complying with their requirements regarding political prisoners. Such harm would amount to persecution for a Convention ground if his claim were well-founded. Credibility and State Protection

The claimant submitted a psychiatric assessment which is discussed more at length below. I mention it here as the diagnosis of the doctor in Canada cannot substitute for the panel's credibility assessment of the claimant. However, the doctor notes that the claimant suffers from anxiety and depression. The panel attempted to question the claimant with sensitivity to this diagnosis. Furthermore, counsel brought to my attention the clear weight loss suffered by the claimant6 and noted that persons suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder often have recall problems or problems in concentration.

The panel did not notice the claimant had any particular problem with his ability to recall or describe events he alleged occurred. The panel did not notice any problems that could be ascribed to a problem of concentration. I note that the psychiatric assessment diagnoses moderate symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder.

I found the claimant's testimony not to be credible with respect to his fear of anti-PA militants for several reasons, mainly because the claimant was employed by the government of Palestine and worked within the military when the alleged problems arose. Intertwined with this finding, I find that the claimant did not avail himself of his state's protection as he is required to do.

The panel first looked at the threats from the Hamas in Palestine that the claimant alleges. The claimant testified he was subjected to threatening phone calls from Hamas on two occasions in 2008. He wrote in his Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative that the callers demanded he cooperate XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

The claimant testified that, after the second threatening call, the caller told him that he had failed them to the point that one of their colleagues had died in intelligence prison because he had XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and that Hamas blamed him for this death. Subsequently, about one month after the death threat, someone shot up his residence and fled the scene by car.

The claimant wrote in his PIF narrative that he went to his "supervisor" each time. In his testimony, the claimant stated he had two superiors, a Captain and a Colonel.7 This is the core of the claim but the description of the officers' response to his concerns is neither cogent or credible. Although the claimant never disclosed his military rank in his PIF,8 the claimant disclosed to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (CIC) in his Background Information form9 filed with his refugee claim, that the claimant set out that he was, from XXXX 2005 to XXXX 2008, a XXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, as well as working for the PA XXXXXXXXXXX XXXX during the same period.

The documentary evidence provided by the Board is found in the national documentation package for Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT) dated 29 November 2010. The OPT is formed of the West Bank (including East Jerusalem) and the Gaza Strip. The Israeli-Palestinian Interim Agreement on the West Bank and the Gaza Strip concluded in September 1995 divided the West Bank into three zones: Area A consisting of approximately 17.2% of the West Bank was under sole Palestinian jurisdiction and security control, although Israel retained authority over access to and from the zone; about 23.8% (Area B) was under Israeli military control, with the PA responsible for civil administration and public order; the remaining 59% (Area C) remained under Israeli military occupation. The total area of the territory over which the PA will eventually assume control, and the extent of its jurisdiction there, remain subject to 'final status' talks. The population of the West Bank is approximately 2.35 million. The vast majority of Palestinians in the OPT are Muslim. Gaza City is the administration centre for the PA and Ramallah is the PA's administrative centre in the West Bank. The status of Jerusalem remains subject to negotiation on so-called 'final status' issues under the Oslo accords.10

According to the UK Report,11 the Palestinian Liberation Organization and Israel established the Palestinian Authority (PA) in 1994. The PA is intended to serve as the governing body of the West Bank and Gaza until a final agreement is reached in the peace process. According to the US Department of State in its introduction to the OPT,12 The Palestinian Authority (PA) has a democratically elected president and legislative council. The president appoints the prime minister who forms a cabinet in consultation with the president; the PA exercised varying degrees of authority over the Palestinian population in the West Bank because of the Israel Defense Force's (IDF) continuing presence, little authority in Gaza, and none over Israeli residents of the West Bank or Arab residents of East Jerusalem. In 2005 Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) Chairman Mahmoud Abbas won 62 percent of the vote in a presidential election regarded as generally free and fair. In 2006 Palestinian Legislative Council (PLC) elections, Hamas, a terrorist organization, backed candidates under the "Reform and Change Movement" ticket and won 74 of 132 seats in elections that generally met democratic standards. In March 2007 Hamas formed a national unity government (NUG) with the Fatah party, but after three months Hamas staged a violent takeover of PA government installations in Gaza and killed hundreds in the Fatah movement and PA security forces. President Abbas then dismissed the NUG and appointed a cabinet of independents led by Prime Minister Salam Fayyad that has governed the West Bank, while elements of the former Hamas government formed the ruling authority in Gaza where it selectively applied the laws and legal structures of the PA. President Abbas and his subordinates controlled PA security forces in the West Bank. Armed militias and terrorist organizations were still active in some areas. In Gaza, Hamas controlled security forces. Other armed factions and terrorist organizations were active in Gaza. The Israeli government maintained effective control of its security forces.

The Economist's backgrounder, as found in the UK Report, noted:13 "Although it lacks many of a sovereign state's common features, Palestine's political system is vibrant and pluralistic, though violent at times. Until June 2007, parts of the West Bank and all of the Gaza Strip, from which Israel withdrew in 2005, were run by the Palestinian Authority (PA). Fatah, the secularist party of the late Yasser Arafat, controlled the PA until a surprising victory by the Islamists of Hamas in the parliamentary election of 2006. "Things have gone downhill since then. Hamas and Fatah, headed by the PA's president, Mahmoud Abbas, hashed out a power-sharing agreement in February 2007. But that deal quickly broke down and internecine fighting resulted in what some fear could be a fatal schism in the territories. Hamas has a grip on Gaza, while Fatah retains control in the West Bank. Efforts at reconciliation have failed, as have efforts from America and Israel to boost Mr Abbas and make life hard for Hamas, which refuses to recognise Israel. In the aftermath of the bloody Gaza war, which deepened the division between these rival factions, foreign diplomacy is needed to mend the Palestinian schism."

Jane's, in its Sentinel Country assessment, updated 22 May 2009, noted14 that: "The Palestinian Territories are effectively divided into two political units: an internationally recognised and accepted Abbas-led West Bank under tight Israeli security control, and a Hamas-led internationally isolated Gaza Strip, in which Israel's presence is confined to air and land incursions. Attempts are underway to bring the two factions together, although unity talks mediated by Egypt have either been rejected by Hamas or ended without agreement. PA forces, concerned that a Gaza-style takeover my be [sic] on the cards for the West Bank, continue to crackdown on Hamas militants and charities. Although possible, Israel, whose forces still control large parts of the West Bank, would undoubtedly prevent Hamas making such a move. Repeated attempts throughout 2008 to reunite the divided factions were unsuccessful, with Hamas refusing to take part in talks set for November 2008. However, in the aftermath of the Israeli campaign in the Gaza Strip, the two sides held their first high level face-to-face meeting in March 2009. Indications are that both sides are willing to compromise and look at the possibility of forming another unity government, but these talks again ended without agreement."

The panel takes a negative credibility inference that the claimant, a Sunni Muslim,15 wrote in his IMM5474 that he feared being killed by Islamists and not the group he stated in his testimony and in his PIF narrative that he feared. The court has stated that inconsistency between Port of Entry notes and the PIF narrative is one way to determine if a claimant is credible, as the first story is often the most credible story.

The claimant works for the PA XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. I find that the claimant's story is not corroborated by the documentary evidence and the claimant has not provided any evidence from his former commanding officer or officers to corroborate his claim. Furthermore, the claimant failed to provide a copy of his military discharge papers or anything else that might assist the panel to find the claim credible.

If the claimant has been asked to comply with improper directions by terrorists (or at least anti-government Islamists), the claimant must do more than say this happened: he is obliged to provide some evidence that this happened through the evidence of another XXXXXXXX, or better from his superiors that he reported it, which he failed to do.

Furthermore, even if the claimant is to be believed that his superiors did nothing for him, the claimant is obliged to do more than merely tell them about the calls and the shooting. He could have filed a complaint. He could have spoken to the PA and its representatives. He could have spoken to the Israeli security authorities, who would have been more interested in those trying to keep political detainees out of prison. There many things the claimant could have done short of fleeing Palestine for Canada. Accordingly, I find that the claimant is not credible and that the claimant failed to avail himself of the protection of the Palestinian Authority.
In regards to the Counsel's submissions regarding Hamas, I note that he has not distinguished the situation in Gaza from that in the West Bank.

The panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee as there is no evidence it would have been unreasonable for the claimant to obtain the protection of his state, or at least engage it more than he did. Psychiatric Assessment

The claimant provided a report dated XXXX 2010 from Dr. XXXXXXXXX, a medical doctor and psychiatrist retained by counsel to provide an assessment for the hearing.16 Dr. XXXXXXX is currently the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (ON) XXXXXXXXXXXX, among other associations listed in his curriculum vitae,17 and is currently in private practice having been XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX from 19XX to 19XX. In addition to his doctorate in medicine, Dr. XXXXXXX has several post-doctoral academic credentials in psychiatry, including a membership in the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and a XXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. As a medical doctor trained in psychiatry, the author of the assessment of XXXXXXX is in a better position to diagnose his condition than many.

The author recounts in his assessment the information provided by the claimant not only in his PIF (which the psychiatrist read) but also in his interview with the author. Additional information provided by Dr. XXXXXXX is that XXXXXXXX suffered a panic attack "about a year ago" (which would place the attack in XXXX of 2009) or about nine months after the claimant entered Canada. Since that time, the assessment indicates that the claimant has been treated with medication and has improved somewhat but is still: "getting similar attacks almost daily lasting from anything like a few minutes to an hour. Even in between attacks he does not feel particularly relaxed.... He has been subject to nightmares ... With regard to his mood, he is sad most of the time and, sometimes, feels like crying. He lacks energy. He does not socialize very much."

There is no previous or family psychiatric history, according to the assessment. Although the claimant reported having some cognitive difficulties particularly with short-term memory and paying attention, this "...seems to have improved."18

The panel notes that Dr. XXXXXXX appears to have seen the claimant only once on XXXX 2010.19 His "...diagnosis according to DSM4TR is...", under Axis I: post-traumatic stress disorder; Axis II: no diagnosis; Axis III: reflux esophagitis; Axis IV: stress from traumatizing events described in the history; Axis V: GAF 60, past year 60.20

The claimant is taking Prevacid 30mg one or two tablets daily for his stomach and Lorazepam 0.5mg daily. Although the assessing psychiatrist indicates that the Prevacid is being used to treat the reflux (Axis III), he does not explain the prescription for Lorazepam or the indications for its use here. Lorazepam is a well-known drug used in the short-term treatment of anxiety, insomnia, acute seizures and sedation of hospitalised patients, as well as sedation of aggressive patients.

The claimant's counsel disclosed several notes and articles, including "Rhyme Of The Ancient Wanderer: a clear and understandable explanation of DSM-IV and it's purpose".21 his article indicates that the DSM-IV stands for "diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders - 4th edition", published in May 1994, referred to as the "'bible' of psychiatric diagnosis because it provides definitions, symptoms and characteristics for mental disorders that are recognized by clinicians from around the world. ... Axis I identifies mental disorders; Axis II identifies personality disorders and mental retardation. Axis III identifies relevant physical diseases and conditions. Axis IV is used by the clinician to assess an individual's overall functioning based on the 100 point scale called the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF)".22

Dr. XXXXXXX does not provide information as to how he arrived at his diagnosis or what tests, if any, he conducted to assist him in his evaluation and assessment. According to Axis I, Dr. XXXXXXX indicates the presence of post-traumatic stress disorder. Outside of the assessment but found in counsel's accompanying material, counsel has flagged various entries in blue with the word "NOTE" and an arrow. For example, under "A complete description of mood disorders" (Axis I), there is a note "Major depression" but no indication if that is a finding of the doctor or an editorial note by counsel. Later for the "GAF" (Axis V), there is a red arrow across from the following notation: 60-51 Moderate symptoms (e.g., flat effect and circumstantial speech, occasional panic attacks) or moderate difficulty in social, occupational, or school functioning (e.g., no friends, unable to keep a job).

The conclusion of the psychiatrist and his prognosis are as follows: "The symptoms described by XXXXXXXX are consistent with the experiences of threats and the attempt on his life he reported to me. I believe his post-traumatic stress disorder will remit if he is allowed to stay in this country and thereby allowed to feel secure that his life will not be threatened again."23

In other words, it appears, but it is not clear from the separation of the notes from the report itself signed by the doctor, that Dr. XXXXXXX concludes that the claimant suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder with "moderate symptoms".24

In "PTSD in Refugees" another article referred to me by counsel, under the title "Traumatic events encountered by refugees",25 the following is noted: Prior to flight, individuals who become refugees may face a wide variety of traumatic events. ... the most commonly reported traumatic event was forced isolation (e.g., ... separation from others). ... In addition to the often life-threatening stresses experienced immediately prior to flight, refugees frequently experience recurring losses, challenges, and changes during the exile/acculturation and resettlement/repatriation periods. ... Having left their homes, refugees are often forced to confront isolation, hostility, violence, and racism in their new locations. ... Additional chronic stressors that refugees must deal with include socioeconomic disadvantages, poor physical health, and the collapse of social support. [Emphasis added by the panel].

The panel member does not possess a doctorate in medicine as Dr. XXXXXXX possesses and certainly is not qualified to dispute his conclusion that the claimant is suffering from depression following his interview; however, the panel cannot conclude that the claimant's depression is a result of what the claimant reported happened to him in Palestine.

There could be many reasons why the claimant may be depressed and anxious, including the factors in bold noted above, such as isolation and hostility in Canada. The panel does not find it unreasonable for a 34 year-old XXXXXXXXXX facing the stresses of a refugee hearing in a strange new land, with the socio-economic disadvantages of being without assets or a job including being without legal authority XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, being without the social support of his close and loving family back home and being without the emotional support of his fiancée, who is in Jordan, to be anxious and depressed. Keeping these other possible factors impacting on the claimant's emotional state, the panel can give little weight to the assessment of Dr. XXXXXXX as a basis for determining that the claimant's stated fears are objectively credible and cannot conclude that Dr. XXXXXXX assessment is sufficient to establish, on balance, that the claimant possesses a subjective well-founded fear of persecution for an imputed political opinion.

The panel can give this report and Dr. XXXXXXX conclusions little weight. The panel notes that Dr. XXXXXXX report is based primarily on what the claimant told him. Given that the panel does not believe the claimant and does not find him credible, the panel finds that the conclusion of the psychiatrist, "The symptoms described by XXXXXXXXX are consistent with the experiences of threats and the attempt on his life he reported to me" are not determinative, as "...such a report cannot possibly serve as a cure-all for any and all deficiencies in a claimant's testimony"26. Risk to Life and Other Serious Harms

Having found that the claimant is not a Convention refugee, the panel then considered whether the harm allegedly feared by the claimant would amount to a risk of life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. There is no evidence before the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant faces such risk.
Furthermore, the claimant's family still lives in XXXXXX and there is no evidence of anything happening to them.

For these reasons set out above, the panel does not find the claimant's allegations that there is no serious possibility that he would face persecution from the Hamas or other Islamist groups. The panel also finds that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant does not face a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture if he were to return to Palestine, for the reasons analyzed above under section 96 of the Act.

For the foregoing reasons, the panel determines that XXXXXXXXXX is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection and therefore rejects his claim. (signed) 'James V. Railton' James V. The panel is aware that the claimant has the burden to establish his claim with "clear, cogent and convincing evidence", which does not raise the standard of proof but merely indicates that a panel must be satisfied the facts in issue are more likely than not to have occurred. Should the panel not be able to determine if a fact in issue is established by the claimant, when it is his burden to do so, then the panel will find the fact has not been established. On the other hand, the panel is aware that, once the facts respecting an allegation of persecution is found, then the panel must determine if, on those facts, there is more than a mere possibility of persecution in the future, that is to say, a "reasonable chance" of persecution for a Convention ground, as set out in Adjei. 5 Exhibit C-2, pages 51-54 6 Exhibit C-2, page 1 (recent photo) compared to pages 53, 55 and 57 (previously) 7 These were not precisely the actual ranks of his supervisors but the best that the claimant and the interpreter could do with the rank the claimant used in Arabic.
